title: Children Helped Make the Middle East's Oldest Clay Figures
summary:
Long before anyone invented pottery, people in the Middle East were already shaping clay into tiny figures. Archaeologists say more than 150 of these artworks, found across present-day Israel, are likely the region's earliest clay figures. And some were made by children.

The figures date back 11,500 to 15,000 years. They were made by the Natufians, hunter-gatherers who lived in the Fertile Crescent between 9,500 and 13,000 BCE and were beginning to settle down and move toward farming.

The figures show birds and hooved mammals like deer, as well as male and female people. Some still carry traces of pigment and dyes. Others carry the ancient fingerprints of their makers. By studying those marks, researchers found that both children and adults helped make the figures.

Clay is not like stone or bone. Earlier Natufian figures were carved from hard materials. Clay needed different skills: shaping soft earth, then baking and hardening it. The findings were published in the journal PLOS One. Laurent Davin of The Hebrew University of Jerusalem said the fingerprints show creativity was shared across generations.
why_it_matters: Seeing that children long ago helped make art shows that your own making and creating matters too, even when you are young.

background_read: Long ago, before people learned to make pots, they shaped soft clay into small figures of animals and people.
Clay is soft earth that can be shaped by hand and then baked until it turns hard, which is different from carving stone or bone.
People who study the past can learn from the tiny fingerprints left in the clay, because they show who made the figures.
